To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

rats can learn about the oral qualities of a food after it is paired with a gastrointestinal (GI)-induced illness and that they can learn about both nutrients and nonnutritives flavors when presented orally.

rats can learn to discriminate between 2 different nutrients (e.g., fat and carbohydrate) and 2 nonnutitive flavors (e.g., cherry and banana) after GI infusion of 1 of these nutrients paired with LiCl, but they can also learn to discriminate between the 4 compounds after oral training with LiCl.
the GI tract is a powerful learning environment that can be used to study the mechanisms that underlie taste aversion learning and flavor preference learning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that taste and flavor play in the development of dietary preferences and food aversions.
the mechanisms underlying the acquisition, retention, and expression of conditioned taste aversions.
how the body processes and learns about food, and we are interested in the neural and behavioral consequences of this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is an interaction between taste and smell, and that this interaction is important in food intake.

the results indicate that rats can learn to discriminate between nutrients and nonnutritives, but not between compounds comprising these stimuli, when they are presented either intestinally, orally, or in both ways.

the results of the present experiments indicate that the processing of nutrients in the GI tract may enhance the salience of nonnutritive oral stimuli, and that this may be a mechanism for nutrient learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the oral properties of nutrients are more salient than their nonnutritive counterparts and that the GI tract can potentiate learning about oral properties.

we have demonstrated that rats can learn to associate the taste and smell of a food with the positive consequences of that food (nutrient absorption) when the food is delivered directly to the gut, and we have demonstrated that the same food is not as well learned when the food is consumed orally.
we are learning that taste and odor can be learned in the gut.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the GI tract is a powerful modulator of learning and memory, and it may be possible to use these mechanisms to enhance learning in the context of food consumption.
the GI tract can be trained to discriminate between flavors.
there is a difference in how animals process nutritive and non-nutritive flavors when the flavors are paired with a gastrointestinal stimulus.
